newsitem.title: MEXICO: Yet another Mexican guerrilla group is born.
newsitem.headline: Yet another Mexican guerrilla group is born.

text.p: A new Mexican group on Wednesday claimed to be the latest in a growing number of would-be leftist guerrilla armies, the third new group since June and the fourth overall in Mexico.

The Armed Front for the Liberation of the Marginalized People of Guerrero (FALPMG) sent a manifesto to the media claiming that it has reunited after several years of lending selected fighters to other guerrilla forces.
Guerrero is a poor state in the southwest of Mexico.

"As of this moment we begin pressure tactics so that we are heard ... and most importantly we initiate a project that carries with it the proposal ... to seek a solution to the inconformities brought forth by the peasants and marginalized Indians of the state of Guerrero," the statement said.
The statement was made available to Reuters late on Wednesday. Authorities could not be immediately reached for comment.
Of the three self-proclaimed guerrilla groups to have emerged this year, only one, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), has been known to carry out attacks.
The EPR has launched sneak attacks on army and police targets in several states, including installations just outside Mexico City. About 25 people have died and nearly 50 have been injured.
Last month, the self-styled Revolutionary Army of Popular Insurgence (ERIP) declared itself "an army of the people and for the people," but so far has not carried out any attacks.

The three new groups join the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN), which introduced itself on Jan. 1, 1994, by occupying several cities in the southeastern state of Chiapas, directly confronting the Mexican army for 10 days. An estimated 145 people died in the fighting.
The Zapatistas, who are primarily Maya Indians, have been in peace talks with the Mexican government for more than 18 months.
Zapatista leader Subcommander Marcos, the masked, pipe-smoking intellectual who has gained worldwide fame, warned last month that three or four new guerrilla bands have sprung up in Mexico.
